scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Muthappan worship originated in the northern Malabar region of Kerala, India, particularly in the village of Eruvessy in Kannur district.
The deity is believed to be a personification of two divine figures, Thiruvappan and Vellatom, representing Shiva and Vishnu.
The Thiyyar community of Malabar performs all rituals and rites for Muthappan, considering him their ancestral deity.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Muthappan Theyyam is performed year-round in northern Kerala.
The annual Ulsavam festival at Parassinikkadavu Madappura begins with a procession led by a male member of the Thayyil clan of the Thiyyar community.
The deity is worshipped with offerings including toddy and fish, reflecting local customs.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Thiyyar community plays a central role in Muthappan worship as ritual performers and priests.
The Thayyil clan leads the annual Ulsavam festival procession at Parassinikkadavu.
Muthappan temples and worship exist primarily in Kannur and Kasaragod districts of Kerala and Coorg district of Karnataka.
Muthappan is a syncretic deity embodying Shiva and Vishnu, represented as Thiruvappan (Valiya Muthappan) and Vellatom (Cheriya Muthappan).

images.description:
Theyyam or Theyyaattam is a pattern of hero worship performed in Kolathunaad, a territory comprising the present Cannanore District and Badagara Taluk of Kerala State (North Kerala). It is a ritual and a folk-dance form supported by a vast literature of folk songs. Theyyam is a corruption for Deyvam - ‘God’. 'Aattam' means dance. Thus 'Theyyaattam' means the God’s Dance.

Madappuras, the temples dedicated to Muthappan, do not have idols or temple flagstaffs but are open-air shrines where the Theyyam is performed. Dogs are present in and around the temple, symbolizing the deity's companions.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Muthappan Theyyam is performed year-round in northern Kerala. The annual Ulsavam festival at Parassinikkadavu Madappura begins with a procession led by a male member of the Thayyil clan of the Thiyyar community. The deity is worshipped with offerings including toddy and fish, reflecting local customs. Muthappan is regarded as a protector of marginalized communities and is worshipped inclusively, with temple entry open to all castes and religions, including Muslims who participate in festivals.
